units.text: 5. The Crowd, the Citizen, and the Invisible Hands
Why Does Nobody Help—and Why Might the Question Be Wrong?

Someone collapses in a railway station. Twenty people are nearby. Each sees that the others see. Each might assume someone else has already called for help. A photograph of the scene could become evidence of modern indifference. But the photograph does not tell us who intervened a moment earlier, who is looking for a phone, who has not understood what is happening, or whether the situation is actually an emergency. Moral judgment needs more than a convincing frame.

In John Darley and Bibb Latané’s classic experiment, published in 1968, participants heard someone apparently having a seizure over a communication system. Intervention depended on how many other witnesses they believed were present. The study helped formulate the idea of diffusion of responsibility: the perceived presence of others can weaken the feeling that you, specifically, must act. Yet this was a precise experimental situation, not a definitive X-ray of human character. [ 23 ]

A meta-analysis published by Peter Fischer and colleagues in 2011, involving more than 7,700 participants and 105 independent effect estimates, found an overall bystander effect: the likelihood of individual intervention could decline in the presence of others. But the results depended on context. In situations perceived as dangerous, the effect was attenuated; others could also represent support, not merely an excuse for passivity. [ 24 ]

A very different investigation requires further caution. Richard Philpot and colleagues analyzed 219 recordings of public conflicts in three cities. At least one bystander intervened in approximately 91% of incidents. More bystanders were associated with a higher probability that someone would help. The study concerned visible conflicts in monitored spaces, not every imaginable emergency, and did not establish that every intervention resolved the situation. [ 25 ]

The two kinds of finding do not automatically contradict each other. The probability that a particular person will help is not the same as the probability that at least one of those present will help. Ten people, each less willing, may together offer more chances of intervention than a single person. The exact relationships depend on their interactions; the logical distinction remains valid.

This difference also changes the moral discussion. We cannot infer from the existence of diffusion of responsibility that crowds are inevitably cruel. Nor does the frequency of helping in certain conflicts mean we can comfortably rely on someone else. Describing a mechanism does not grant an individual an exemption. It shows where coordination can fail and where it is worth building.

Let us return to the station. One bystander explicitly asks whether help has been called. Another answers. A third looks for station staff. The situation is resolved not by a sudden increase in everyone’s virtue but by turning a diffuse obligation into identifiable actions. This is a hypothetical example, not a universal recipe for emergencies. The general idea is that responsibility sometimes needs a clear sentence before it needs a moral speech.

The same problem arises in public administration. A report reaches five departments. Each registers it; none is tasked with checking the final outcome. All can demonstrate that they followed their procedure, while the affected person remains without an answer. The failure need not be explained exclusively by officials’ malice. It may be produced by an organizational structure that distributes activities but not the obligation to follow their consequences.

Hence a simple institutional requirement: for foreseeable problems, there must be a connection between a report, a decision, and verification. Someone must be able to say not only “I passed it on” but also “I checked what happened.” That person must be given time and authority. Naming someone responsible without providing the necessary means is an elegant way to prepare a scapegoat.

Yet clarity of roles must not produce indifference outside them. “It is not my department” can be useful information or an abdication. The difference depends on what follows: do I point to a functioning route or close the conversation? I do not owe a solution to every problem I encounter. I may owe its proper transfer when doing so is simple and abandoning it would cause foreseeable harm.
The Order, the Uniform, and the Promise That Someone Else Knows

Another scene: a participant believes that, at a researcher’s request, he is administering electric shocks to someone. Stanley Milgram’s 1963 experiment became one of the best-known images of obedience. In the classic condition, 26 of the 40 male participants proceeded to the maximum indicated level. The shocks were not real, but participants had not been told this. The figure of 65% describes that condition, not a universal proportion of people willing to torture. [ 26 , 27 ]

The interpretation of the experiments remains debated. Stephen Reicher and Alexander Haslam have argued that identification with the scientific purpose and the experimenter’s authority explains some findings better than the image of completely blind obedience. Experimental conditions produced important variations. This reinterpretation does not establish that people are immune to authority; it challenges an overly simple explanation of how authority works. [ 27 ]

For responsibility, the difference is crucial. Someone may participate in harm not only by abandoning every moral purpose but also by adopting a supposedly higher one: progress, saving the organization, the group’s security. “We are doing this for good” can close down scrutiny of the means at precisely the moment it should intensify it.

Suppose a team accepts a minor violation to save an important project. Then a second arises, justified by the investment already made. By the end, members see themselves not as people who chose wrong, but as people who defended something valuable against obstacles. The scenario does not establish how frequently this happens. But it shows why sincerity of conviction is insufficient to justify action.

Responsible authority must allow itself to be challenged without turning every objection into betrayal. At the same time, a team cannot function if every decision remains suspended until every member is completely convinced. The solution is not the absence of authority but differentiating decisions: some require rapid execution, others independent scrutiny, and some must be stopped when serious signs of harm appear. These thresholds must be considered before the crisis, not improvised afterward to protect management.

Groups can also support responsibility. Robert Sampson and colleagues’ research on “collective efficacy” linked trust among neighbors and willingness to intervene for the common good with lower levels of neighborhood violence. The Chicago study was observational: associations, even after statistical adjustments, are not equivalent to experimental evidence that simply increasing trust automatically produces safety. In his later analysis, Sampson also emphasizes resources and the wider context. [ 28 , 29 ]

The moral conclusion is not that residents of a poor neighborhood are to blame for failing to produce enough solidarity. That would conveniently invert the problem. Cooperation requires material conditions, time, stability, and institutions that deserve a measure of trust. Asking neighbors to compensate alone for the absence of public services means privatizing a collective obligation.

Nor is solidarity good by definition. A tightly united group can protect an aggressor, exclude a newcomer, or conceal abuse to preserve its reputation. We must ask not only how much people cooperate, but for what purpose and against whom. Mature collective responsibility requires bonds strong enough for action and rights solid enough to limit group pressure.

A good community is not one in which nobody can say “no.” It is one in which a reasoned refusal can become useful information rather than evidence of impurity. Sometimes the person who temporarily weakens a group’s apparent unity protects precisely the conditions for cooperation worth preserving.
Citizenship Is Not a Certificate of Innocence

A citizen says: “I did not decide. I did not sign. I did not benefit.” Sometimes all three claims are true. The question is whether it follows that there is nothing left for that citizen to do. It does not automatically follow, because responsibility for the future is not identical to blame for the past.

Philosophical discussions of collective responsibility distinguish attributing actions to a group from distributing obligations among its members. They also examine whether organizations, not merely individuals, can be responsible agents. There is no unanimously accepted solution. One important point, however, is separating the obligation to remedy a common problem from the assumption that every member personally committed the same injustice. [ 30 ]

Suppose a city spent decades building services that exclude people with reduced mobility. A new resident did not design the steps, refuse funding, and perhaps did not even know about the problem. That person is not the author of that past. But as a participant in current institutions, they may have reasons to support transforming them. The obligation need not be grounded in inherited guilt; it can be grounded in the present need to build an accessible order.

Likewise, benefiting from an advantage created through injustice does not automatically make you morally identical to its perpetrator. But it may matter to how the costs of repair should be shared. This is a thesis requiring arguments and evidence in each situation: what advantage persists, who bears the disadvantage, what measure would actually correct the problem, and whom would it burden? Historical labels alone do not answer these questions.

Citizenship involves a further difficulty: nobody can understand every public issue in depth. Someone working long hours, caring for another person, and struggling with difficulties of their own does not have the same capacity to become informed as a well-funded institution. Requiring universal expertise before recognizing their right to an opinion would be a form of exclusion.

Yet lack of expertise does not justify every kind of conduct. There is a difference between not knowing a case and confidently spreading an accusation you have made no effort to verify. We can require proportionality between what someone knows, how categorically they speak, and how much influence they wield. The same rumor shared in a private conversation and promoted by an organization with a large audience does not create the same situation of responsibility.

A society cannot depend solely on impeccable citizens. It needs rules limiting the harm caused by foreseeable mistakes, intelligible public information, and opportunities for correction. Institutions should not be designed for a fictional citizen who is infinitely attentive, perfectly rational, and always rested. Nor should they be designed for a citizen treated as permanently incapable of judgment.

There is also responsibility for not accepting every obligation claimed in the community’s name. A state may demand unjust sacrifices, a majority may demand a minority’s silence, and an organization may confuse loyalty with obedience. Answering to others does not mean surrendering the right to ask who makes the demand and who benefits from it.

Responsible citizenship is therefore neither complete withdrawal into private life nor permanent mobilization. It is limited but real participation in maintaining our shared world, accompanied by the right to refuse abusive demands. How extensive that participation should be remains an open moral question. The fact that we cannot set a perfect quota does not make every contribution optional.
